articles.text: San Francisco and Berkeley lifted their proof-of-vaccination requirement for patrons of indoor commercial spaces on Friday, March 11. It is unclear when Alameda County will follow suit. The City and County of San Francisco announced on March 9 that it will no longer require people to provide proof of vaccination or a negative COVID-19 test to enter certain businesses. Businesses may decide to be more restrictive than local guidance. For example, a restaurant owner in San Francisco may still require that patrons show proof of up-to-date vaccination status and wear masks indoors. The health order requiring proof of vaccination was made in San Francisco on August 20, 2021 - six months before the same order was issued in Alameda County. San Francisco was the first city in the nation to make such a requirement. Berkeley followed suit soon after, making a similar requirement in September. The Health Order in San Francisco was authored and recommended to city officials by the San Francisco Department of Public Health (SFDPH), and approved by San Francisco Mayor London Breed and Director of Health Dr. Grant Colfax. In Berkeley, the order came from the city’s own public health department. The timeline of when Oakland’s (and other Alameda County cities excluding Berkeley) requirement will be lifted is unclear. That’s because most cities in Alameda County align with directives from the Alameda Department of Public Health, but that agency will not be providing directives on when to lift the requirement - in the situation of Oakland, it will come directly from Oakland City Council. Guidance will come when the City of Oakland’s Declaration of Local Emergency is lifted by Oakland’s City Council, a decision that will not be directly influenced by the Alameda County Health Department (ACPHD), confirmed Communications Specialist Sonia Painda. In Oakland, the requirement went into effect on February 1 under a directive by Oakland’s City Council, based upon an ordinance sponsored by Councilmember Dan Kalb. Councilmember Kalb did not immediately return request for comment. “The city of Oakland does not have a public health department. We have aligned with Alameda County [Public Health Department],” Oakland Citywide Communications Director Karen Boyd confirmed. “The City Council would have to take action to reverse that ordinance. There is no timeline, because we are still in the midst of the COVID emergency.”

articles.text: The weekend of March 12-13 was a boon to Piedmont teens. Piedmont Community Church held its annual Treasures Sale and raised $19,000 for its annual Youth Service Trip during Spring Break to build homes in Mexico. The youth and adult leadership are excited to be able to plan for the trip the week of April 11-15. The church-sponsored trip was canceled the last two years due to COVID. The large fundraiser at the church venue was sized down this year for safety precautions. In 2019 the sale raised more than $38,000. The 2020 sale was one of the last events to happen in Piedmont before the shelter in place was ordered on March 15, 2020 and raised $30,000, although the 2020 trip in April was canceled at the last minute. The funds pay for the supplies needed to build the houses in Mexico, allowing the construction to be done at no cost to the recipients. Funds also are used for scholarships for students to take part on the six-day trip service project. “We were very fortunate to raise $19,000, because last year we could not have the sale,” said Rev. Scott Kail, the church’s Youth Minister. “We had a meeting Sunday in our church sanctuary with everyone involved in the Mexico trip. Everyone was thrilled and very excited about going.”

articles.text: Piedmont Community Church named Dr. Steve Schibsted as its new Senior Pastor on Sunday, March 6. He has served 14 months as the church’s Transitional Pastor following the retirement of Rev. Dr. Bill McNabb who served as Senior Minister for 20 years. He was selected following the recommendation of a Pastor Nominating Committee, co-chaired by Eric Behrens and Zookie Todd, and by consensus vote by parishioners in the church on March 6. He gave his first sermon as the church’s new Transitional Minister on January 3, 2021. Rev. Schibsted has over 20 years of experience working in churches much larger than Piedmont Community Church. A Southern California native, his first experience with the Presbyterian Church was as a youth intern in Santa Barbara, which led to leadership roles in youth ministries at Mount Hermon near Rev. articles.text: The City of Piedmont will host a virtual discussion on equitable real estate practices that support an inclusive community on April 7 via Zoom. The event, entitled “Welcome to Piedmont: Real Estate Practices in Support of an Inclusive Community,” is co-sponsored by the Piedmont League of Women Voters (LWV), Piedmont Anti-Racism and Diversity Committee (PADC), and Piedmont Racial Equity Campaign (PREC). The discussion will be moderated by Piedmont resident Carol Galante, founder of the Terner Center for Housing Innovation at UC Berkeley. Panelists will include retired Piedmont real estate agent Maureen Kennedy, a member of the Clinton Administration; Chief Diversity and Equity Officer at California Association of Realtors Farrah Wilder; and Community Outreach Coordinator for California Housing Finance Agency (CalHFA) Ashley Gardner. Residents and real estate professionals who tune in will learn about what the current context is for real estate practices and its impact on the demographics of the Piedmont community. articles.text: Join the League of Women Voters of Piedmont (LWV) on Wednesday, March 30, for a discussion with Dr. Fiona Hill, an expert on Russia and a Senior Fellow at The Brookings Institution at Stanford. The Zoom episode will explore the current state of democracy, from both domestic and international points of view. Dr. Hill is the Robert Bosch Senior Fellow at the Center on the United States and Europe in the Foreign Policy program at the Brookings Institution and member of the Council on Foreign Relations. Her most recent book, There is Nothing for You Here, draws on her personal journey out of poverty, as well as her unique perspectives as a historian and policy maker, to show how we can return hope to our forgotten places. From 2017 to 2019 , Dr. Hill served as deputy assistant to the president and senior director for European and Russian affairs on the National Security Council. From 2006 to 2009, she served as national intelligence officer for Russia and Eurasia at the National Intelligence Council. She has researched and published extensively on issues related to Russia, the Caucasus, Central Asia, regional conflicts, energy, and strategic issues. Co-author of Mr. Putin: Operative in the Kremlin and The Siberian Curse: How Communist Planners Left Russia Out in the Dr. Fiona Hill is the guest speaker of a League of Women Voters discussion on Russia on March 30. Cold, she holds a master’s degree in Soviet studies and a doctorate in history from Harvard University and a master’s in Russian and modern history from St. Andrews University in Scotland. This event is part of the League’s 2022 Defending Democracy Speaker Series and is co-sponsored by local Leagues in California, Oregon, Colorado, and Florida. This talk will be held live on Zoom and YouTube and will include an audience question and answer session. Visit the website lwvpiedmont.org to learn more about the series and register for this event. Once you have registered, you will receive the Zoom link by email. The event is free and open to the public.

articles.text: Chalk art, scavenger hunt, and kid-friendly activities Piedmont’s annual Arbor Day celebration will take place on Thursday, April 28, the day prior to National Arbor Day. Arbor Day was held virtually in 2021 due to the COVID pandemic, but all the usual festivities will return live this year. The Piedmont Park Commission will host “gratitude trees” in Crocker Park and Piedmont Park. During the week of April 24-29, residents and kids are invited to write messages on tags to place on trees. Tags can be picked up at City Hall and at the Recreation Department. The Park Commission will sponsor a movie in Piedmont Park, a documentary entitled Intelligent Trees to be shown at 8:30 p.m. on April 28 in the Main Park. There will be popcorn and refreshments for the film. Special additions this year include more kid-friendly activities. At its most recent meeting, the Park Commission discussed plans to revive last year’s tree-related sidewalk chalk art, which will again be hosted by Piedmont’s Public Works Department. Young participants will choose their favorite public tree and include the name of the species in their drawing. Those who would like help identifying trees should contact Parks and Projects Manager Nancy Kent at nkent@ piedmont.ca.gov. “It’s a fun and creative way for young residents to get involved in Arbor Day activities,” Park Commission Chair Patty Dunlap said. “[Arbor Day] activities have been more geared toward adults. With [Park Commissioners] Robin Wu and Amber Brumfiel’s push, we’re reaching a different level of residents,” said Commissioner Betty Goodman. There will also be a kidfriendly scavenger hunt. With more than 80 species of public trees in Piedmont, the city’s urban forest will make for an excellent and challenging hunt. “We’re going to have the community thinking about trees for at least five days – hopefully longer,” Dunlap said. Will, Finn and Max Brumfiel participated in last year’s sidewalk chalk art displays celebrating Piedmont’s many tree species on Arbor Day. Piedmont, by Piedmont, for Piedmont. articles.text: Wildfire season hit California hard this year. Climate-change-fueled fires are burning across the state in record size and number, devastating communities and turning the skies red with smoke. During these times, it is easy to feel helpless, especially when the underlying causes of these crises are so monumental. What can ordinary people possibly do to address each other’s health and survival? The Common Humanity Collective (CHC) might have the beginnings of an answer. CHC came together at the beginning of the pandemic as a small group of friends, neighbors, and UC Berkeley graduate students to create alternative ways to produce and distribute hand sanitizer and high-filtration face masks in the Bay Area when these basic resources had disappeared from store shelves. CHC’s momentum grew as more people joined the effort, eventually to over 300 volunteers. They coalesced into decentralized groups across the Bay to build PPE and slow the spread of COVID-19. So far, CHC has distributed over 60,000 DIY “N80” face masks and over 7,000 gallons of sanitizer – all for free. Efforts to make CHC’s masks continued in 2022 and even spread across the country to organizations who heard about CHC from the It Could Happen Here podcast. Recognizing the harmful effects of smoke and air pollutants during the wildfire crisis, the collective has also built high-quality Do It Yourself (DIY) air purifiers so individuals and families can filter the poisonous air that billows into their homes. Since the first signs of smoke in the summer, community members, students, teachers, organizers, tenants, and workers of the East Bay have come together every other Saturday to build these air purifiers and deliver them to the most Elaine Qian distributes an air purifier to a community member in East Oakland who has asthma. affected parts of their communities. More than 130 people from 10 different Bay Area organizations have participated in these builds. The effort has grown to include members of the tenant union Tenant and Neighborhood Councils, the East Bay and SF chapters of the Democratic Socialists of America, the Sunrise Movement, Mask Oakland, other mutual aid groups, as well as friends and families. The DIY purifiers are comparable to significantly more expensive commercial purifiers and can filter a room full of smoke and particulates down to healthy levels within a similar period of time as commercial products. CHC distributes purifiers to the most polluted and least-resourced communities in Oakland and Berkeley, occasionally in partnership with organizations such as East Oakland Collective and Tenant and Neighborhood Councils. The group also makes a determined effort to recruit the recipients of the purifiers to participate in future builds and personally distribute purifiers they assemble to neighbors. Traditional nonprofits that act as a stopgap measure against government austerity often have a demobilizing effect on the beneficiaries of their goodwill. This can perpetuate a cycle of alienation. By urging people to assume ownership of the processes of production and distribution of these essential tools, the work of mutual aid increases their autonomy and their participation in decisions that affect their survival. The attendance at each build event has increased each week with over 1,300 high-quality purifiers assembled and given out so far. What can we do when faced with smoke in our skies from wildfires? Common Humanity Collective says: come together. One person can make a difference, but a community can make a vastly greater difference. We can exercise our collective agency and grow strong together, in the process forging the social relations necessary for the fight toward a better future. Elaine Quian is a PHS class of 2014 graduate and former president of the Piedmont Community Service Crew. CHC volunteers teach community members in East Oakland how to make air purifiers and then give the purifies to residents.

articles.text: In Piedmont School Board’s March 9 meeting, school administrators and teachers reported the results from the February social-emotional health screener. The survey was given to students in grades 3-12 and showed the same percentages of students in each mental health risk category when compared to the survey in September. Based on answers to 28 questions, students scores put them into one of three levels of risk for mental health: “normal risk,” “elevated risk,” and “extremely-elevated risk.” In the fall and in February 86% of students in the district were classified as normal risk, 11% at elevated risk and 3% at extremely-elevated risk for social-emotional health concerns. SEPTEMBER 2021 FEBRUARY 2022 Students at Millennium High School took a field trip in February – their first in two years – to repair a transitional housing facility in Oakland. Principal Shannon Fierro said the project was an example of a school activity boosting students’ mental health. “We are within the normal range, but we know some students in the normal [risk] range are having challenges,” acknowledged curriculum Director Cheryl Wozniak. The test administered was the BASC-3 Behavioral and Emotional Screening System (BESS), first given to Piedmont students in September of 2020 due to concerns over mental health during distance learning. The test results can be further broken down into the following separate indexes: • Internalizing Risk: Locus of control, social stress, anxiety, depression, and sense of inadequacy. A sample question is “I worry but I don’t know why.” • S el f- Re g u l a t io n R i s k : Self-control, hyperactivity and attention problems. A sample question is “I have trouble sitting still.” • Personal Adjustment Risk: Relations with parents, interpersonal relations, self-esteem, and self-reliance. The data is reviewed by principals, counselors, and school psychologists, and is shared with the parents and teachers of students with elevated scores. Middle school students who have been in the elevated or extremely-elevated risk categories for a second iteration of the survey are offered group counseling. Teachers of students falling in one of these categories for the first time are instructed to provide additional attention, and positive reinforcement. Piedmont Principals agreed that the most effective aspect of the survey was that the results allowed them to identify students individually. PHS Principal Adam Littlefield identified some of the limitations of the survey. “We have had some students in the ‘normal risk’ that were hospitalized for self-harm, so it is one of those things that is a piece of information, but is not the end all,” said Littlefield. Littlefield also noted that some students were answering the questions in a way to avoid talking with an adult, essentially bypassing intervention. articles.text: In its March 9 meeting the Piedmont School Board approved issuing advance layoff notices to classified employees due to a lack of work or lack of funds. The position most affected is that of Health Clerk, with the equivalent of approximately four full-time salaries being reduced. “In 2021-22, the District hired several health clerks and instructional aides with one-time grants. The funding is not available for the 2022-23 school year, requiring [the] Board [to] reduce the positions so that lay-off notices can be provided,” said Superintendent Randy Booker. The district currently employs eight health clerks. “Of that total, six are regular employees who will receive notices for part or all of their [salary],” said district CFO Ruth Alahydoian. The other two Health Clerks were already on short-term contracts. These notices must be delivered earlier than in the past due to a change in California Education Code 45117. California schools are now required to give layoff notices for the following year by March 15 to Classified Employees. Previously schools gave 60-day notices. The layoffs are projected. Official notices will be delivered in May. The district is required to give this advance notice telling employees that they likely will not be employed. “In May we will determine whether or not there will be different funding for the following year, or if different work [is] needed. We don’t know where we will be with COVID in May or August, so this just gives us flexibility,” Booker explained. School Board Vice President Megan Pillsbury attended a meeting with Classified Employees and was heartened by the communication the district provided. “I was grateful to hear that the district is making good efforts to find other areas to employ some of these people. Hopefully that can happen with some of the staff that is being laid off,” she said.
articles.title: School District gives advance layoff notices to classified employees

articles.text: In a letter dated March 2, 2022 to parents of Piedmont Middle School students, middle school Principal Ryan Fletcher wrote: It is with mixed emotions that I share with you that I will not be returning to Piedmont Middle School next year. My wife Laura and I have decided to relocate our family to Denver, Colorado. We will be joining a wonderful network of friends and family there, and I will be taking on the position of principal at a small middle school in a suburb outside of Denver. I am so grateful for all that I have learned and gained during my time at PMS. As I begin this next chapter and enter a new school community, I can only hope to feel as embraced and supported as I have been throughout my time in Piedmont. While Laura and I are excited to plant new roots in Colorado, we are sad to end this chapter in Piedmont and will forever feel connected to our time and our experience as part of this special community. I want to assure you that in my final months at PMS I will remain committed to the site goals and initiatives that are currently underway, and I will dedicate my time and energy to supporting the transition to Piedmont Middle School’s next principal. pages.text: Wednesday, March 16, 2022 7 School District gives advance layoff notices to classified employees By Jay Russell In its March 9 meeting the Piedmont School Board approved issuing advance layoff notices to classified employees due to a lack of work or lack of funds. The position most affected is that of Health Clerk, with the equivalent of approximately four full-time salaries being reduced. “In 2021-22, the District hired several health clerks and instructional aides with one-time grants. The funding is not available for the 2022-23 school year, requiring [the] Board [to] reduce the positions so that lay-off notices can be provided,” said Superintendent Randy Booker. The district currently employs eight health clerks. “Of that total, six are regular employees who will receive notices for part or all of their [salary],” said district CFO Ruth Alahydoian. The other two Health Clerks were already on short-term contracts. These notices must be delivered earlier than in the past due to a change in California Education Code 45117. California schools are now required to give layoff notices for the following year by March 15 to Classified Employees. Previously schools gave 60-day notices. The layoffs are projected. Official notices will be delivered in May. The district is required to give this advance notice telling employees that they likely will not be employed. “In May we will determine whether or not there will be different funding for the following year, or if different work [is] needed. We don’t know where we will be with COVID in May or August, so this just gives us flexibility,” Booker explained. School Board Vice President Megan Pillsbury attended a meeting with Classified Employees and was heartened by the communication the district provided. “I was grateful to hear that the district is making good efforts to find other areas to employ some of these people. Hopefully that can happen with some of the staff that is being laid off,” she said. articles.text: What are the chances of an asteroid or a comet impacting Earth? Chabot astronomers have received a lot of questions on the topic after the recent release of the Netflix film Don’t Look Up, centered around an Earth-ending comet. Here’s the good news: there is no known asteroid big enough to cause a global impact that is estimated to hit Earth in the next 100 years. An asteroid would need to be larger than 460 feet to have significant global effects upon impact. Okay, so a big asteroid is likely not coming anytime soon. But how often do small asteroids impact Earth? It turns out, bits of asteroids and comets hit Earth’s atmosphere and burn up all the time. Approximately 80-100 tons of space dust and small meteorites fall on Earth each day. This is what causes “shooting stars”. Recently, a very small asteroid (estimated at less than 7 feet) made impact near Iceland on March 11. Named asteroid 2022 EB5, it was discovered 2 hours before impact by the Konkoly Observatory and became the 5th asteroid to be found before impacting Earth. Did the asteroid land in the ocean? Probably not. Asteroid 2022 EB5 was estimated to be moving about 11 miles per second. When plummeting against the Earth’s speed of 18 miles per second, it likely burned up into a fireball. Some people in Iceland said they caught a bright flash of light or heard a boom. Asteroids like these and comets that can pass within approximately 30 million miles of Earth’s orbit are categorized as Near Earth Objects (NEOs). How many Near Earth Objects are out there now? NASA is currently tracking more than 28,000 and reporting detailed information on Original reporting and mapping by Bill Grey at Project Pluto. their locations. While there is no known global asteroid threat, tracking remains key to understanding and planning for any possible scenario. It is estimated that only about 40 percent of asteroids 460 feet and larger have been found to date and we find around 500 large NEOs like these per year. In fact, around 30 new asteroids are discovered each week by NASA’s NEOWISE spacecraft and ground telescopes around the World. In fact, Chabot Space & Science Center helps with asteroid tracking using our most powerful telescope, Nellie. In July 2008, Chabot Space & Science Center’s 36-inch telescope, Nellie, was officially designated Observatory G-58 by the International Astronomical Union’s Minor Planet Center (MPC) and selected to contribute to its Near Earth Object (NEO) detection and tracking program. To get involved with asteroid tracking, look at The International Astronomical Search Collaboration (IASC). This program puts high-quality data into the hands of citizen scientists around the World, creating opportunities for original astronomical discoveries and hands-on astronomical exploration. Mary Catherine Frantz IS Marketing and Communication Manager at Chabot Space & Science Center is a non-profit institution, community resource, and hub for interactive STEAM engagement in Oakland. Founded in 1883, Chabot’s mission is to inspire and educate learners of all ages about the universe and planet Earth.

The Morisot sisters Édouard Manet was already a cause celebré when Berthe Morisot and her sister Edma were introduced to him by a mutual friend, painter Henri Fantin-Latour who had intimated the sisters were noticeably promising painters. Édouard wrote to Fantin-Latour that, “they’re delightful sisters,” but “what a pity they can’t be men.” He was clearly annoyed by the waste of art training on women. To date, no women had been recognized as serious artists, and yet he was astounded by their confidence and ambition. Edma and Berthe enjoyed all the advantages that the Victorian era could possibly provide. They were intelligent and educated. Their father was an architect in government service and their mother was a distant relative of the rococo Jean-Honoré Fragonard and supported their daughters’ enthusiasm for art instruction. The parents built a studio at home and enlisted A-list artists, especially the Barbizon trailblazer Jean-Baptiste-Camille Corot who praised the girls for their quick learning and skills. Berthe qualified for the annual Impressionist exhibition at age 23, and as she matured, she exhibited her work yearly for more than a decade. Her painting style was loose with fast brushwork radiating confidence, but she was shadowed by self-doubt. articles.text: Piedmont’s boys’ lacrosse team continued its strong start to the season, defeating University of San Francisco 20-11 at Witter Field on Friday, March 11. The Highlanders are undefeated at 4-0 and have scored at least 18 goals in each game. “Overall, it was a very good game for us. We’re improving every game. Our offense is very potent for a young team. We’ve seen a lot of improvement across the board and we’re going to need it. We’re going to play some very difficult opponents in the coming weeks. The boys have really gelled together as a family,” said first-year coach Alex Yu. PHS has now scored 74 goals and allowed 35 through four games. A plethora of scoring options was on display Friday Staff Photos Jack Nelson had a 3-goal hat trick, including a behind-the-back shot in the fourth quarter. Freshman goalie Gus von Metzsch had 15 saves against the Red Devils. Soren Dixon scored eight goals and had two assists and one ground ball recovery in Piedmont’s 20-11 win over University. night. University entered with a 4-1 overall record and is a strong Division 2 team. It faced Piedmont in the 2019 North Coast Section Semifinals, which PHS won 10-5 and went on to win the NCS championship. This year’s team may have more scoring options than in 2019; perhaps proving THAT Piedmont deserved its promotion to Division 1 with large-enrollment schools. “We try to preach selfless ball. The teams that go far in the playoffs are the ones who share the ball. We call it ‘finding the onemore,’ the one extra pass to find the person who is open. They are very good at that,” said Yu. Soren Dixon led the scoring with eight goals against the Red Devils; Nathan Fredericks had six goals, and Jack Nelson had a hat trick (3 goals) including a flashy, no-look goal in the fourth quarter. “It was a beautiful pass when I was running across the field. It was too late for me to do an overhand shot, so I had to go around the back. It just happened in the moment,” explained Nelson. Piedmont freshman goalie Gus von Metzsch continued to impress with 15 saves. “Gus came out tonight. He probably had his best game of the season. Some of his saves were up-close and point blank. His clearing has been stellar as well. I couldn’t be happier to have him, he’s a great teammate,” said Yu of the freshman. University Recap Piedmont jumped ahead 6-1 after one period and led 9-3 by halftime. It outscored the Red Devils 3-2 in the third quarter, and added eight more goals in the fourth for the 20-11 victory. Final stats: Dixon had eight goals, two assists, and one ground ball recovery. Fredericks had six goals. Jack Nelson had three goals, one assist, and one ground ball. Rylan Nelson had two goals, two assists, and two ground balls. Logan Huh scored once, Andrew McLaughlin gained an assist. Tuesday vs. Marin Academy Piedmont traveled to Kentfield to play Marin Academy yesterday, March 15. See next week’s Post for game details. NEXT UP Piedmont (4-0) heads to archrival Bishop O’Dowd in Oakland this Friday, March 18 for a game at 7:00 p.m.

articles.text: Epstein strikes out 11 in 7-1 win against San Leandro Staff Photos Izzy Epstein pitched Piedmont to a 7-1 win over San Leandro. Piedmont’s softball team defeated San Leandro 7-1 on Tuesday, March 15, but was shut out 1-0 by Skyline on Friday, March 11. Both were non-league games. It was a strong hitting display on Tuesday when Piedmont, accumulated eight hits against the Pirates. Chiarra Lundin had a double and scored two runs. “Chiarra is one of our seniors and is the No. 3 hitter in the order. We hope for big things for her this season,: said coach Gene Denard. On the mound, Izzy Epstein pitched a complete game, striking out 11 batters while holding San Leandro to 3 hits and one walk. Annabelle Castronovo pitched a complete 7-inning game against Skyline with five strikeouts. “Izzy is our workhorse this year; she’s maybe the best pitcher in our league. Annabelle is a quality No. 2 for us. She won’t throw as often but we’re confident in her when she does,” said Denard. 7-1 win over San Leandro Piedmont scored its first run with two outs in the bottom second when Morgan Hunt smacked a single to centerfield to bring in Epstein from third. PHS added three runs in the bottom of the third when Castronovo led off with a single and Lundin cracked a double to the left field wall. After a fielders’ choice that advanced Castronovo to third, Miya Fujimoto reached on an error to score Castronovo. Gretchen Gerhardy then brought in Fujimoto and Angelina Wu on a sacrifice fly that was dropped by the outfielder, giving the Highlanders a 4-0 lead. In the bottom of the fourth, Wu reached on another error to score Leah Bell with two outs, 5-1. The final two runs were scored in the bottom of the sixth inning with Fujimoto singling in Castronovo, and Lundin stealing home on a hit-and-run. Final stats: Lundin was 1-for-3 with a double, two runs scored, and a stolen base. Bell went 1-for-4 with a run scored, Castronovo was 1-for-3 with a run scored, Fujimoto went 1-for-4 with two RBIs and a run scored. Loss to Skyline PHS allowed the winning run in the top of the third in a game that was close start to finish. Each team had 4 hits. The Highlanders had a chance to score in the bottom of the third with two runners on and one out, but Fujimoto and Julia Banuelos were stranded on first and second. Final stats: Banuelos went 2-for-2 with a walk. Fujimoto went 1-for-3, Wu went 1-for-4. articles.text: Photos by Todd Marshburn Katherine Kinne (13) scored six goals and had two assists against Dougherty Valley. As Piedmont’s girls’ lacrosse team continues to work through its early-season slate of matches against upper Division 1 competition, it beat Dougherty Valley in San Ramon 13-11 for its first victory of the season on Friday, March 11. “The first three games were against some really tough opponents, Cal High, Redwood and Marin Catholic are all big-time lacrosse programs; the girls finally clicked in the Dougherty. I set up the schedule against tough opponents to ramp up their lacrosse IQ. I think they finally are seeing each other and playing like a team,” explained coach Carlton Chan. Senior attacker Katherine Kinne tied a career-high six goals against Dougherty Valley, and goalies Sofia Ethington and Lindsay Kottle split duties, combining for 9 saves. In the first half, while down 3-0, Kinne got PHS on the board after nearly five minutes of play at 20:19. Elizabeth Ethington made it 3-2 at the 18:14 mark, while Molly Ashton tied it after another three minutes. Kinne put PHS ahead 4-3 at the 13:59 mark, but DV tied it 30 seconds later. At 4-4, Ruby Guzdar scored at 11:54 to put PHS back ahead, but DVHS scored once again just seconds later. Ashton scored again and Kinne scored her third goal 15 seconds later for a 7-5 lead. DV scored again and the teams went into halftime with Piedmont holding a slim 7-6 lead. Dougherty Valley came out firing in the second half, tying it at 7-7 in the first minute of action and then going ahead 8-7. Kinne tied the game after a minute, and then Ashton bagged her third goal with 13:52 on the clock for a 9-8 led. One minute later DV tied the game again. Piedmont’s defense then shut down Dougherty Valley, holding them without a goal for eight minutes. Meanwhile, Kinne and Elizabeth Ethington scored, and Kinne added another goal for a 12-9 lead. DV inched closer , 12019m with 4 minutes left, and scored once more with 1:50 left in the game. However, Piedmont got an insurance goal from Charlotte Theut for the 12-10 final and a hard-earned win. Final stats: Kinne with six goals, two assists, and three ground balls. Elizabeth Ethington and Ashton each had three goals and an assist. Guzdar and Theut had individual goals. articles.text: Piedmont hosted its first league track & field meet of the season on Thursday, March 10 at Witter Field with Hayward, San Leandro, and Tennyson. Her winning time of 10:59.20 in the 3200 smashed her previous personal record by more than 2-1/2 minutes. PHS sophomore Jamie Schwartz, the only other runner, was second in 13:06.17. Also on Saturday, Terrill competed in the pole vault at the K-Bell Classic in Campbell. In a field of 19 vaulters, he placed 3rd with a height of 13 feet, more than one foot below his recent school record vault. articles.text: Piedmont High School’s swim team is back after a two-year halt due to the COVID-19 global pandemic. Both the boys’ and girls’ teams on at the Head-Royce Invitational. The boys came out on top in a field of seven teams, and the girls won in a field of six. Colby Price has returned as head coach In the absence of a pool in Piedmont as a new $19 million facility is being designed, the team will be training at Mills College. “We started with a preseason invitational that we took really seriously and wound up winning, which is fun,” said Price. “We are doing everything we can to get the kids involved. We’re one of the biggest teams at Piedmont High. articles.text: Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir’s Ensemble singers performed with the Oakland Symphony on Friday, March 4 in a program titled Fountains of Rome. The concert honored the memory and life of one of the choir’s most ardent champions and a passionate supporter of the arts and social justice, Bonnie Bonetti-Bell, who died November 20. The loving and personal program celebrated the Oakland Symphony conducting debut of the choir’s Artistic Director, Eric Tuan. Tuan led the singers and orchestra in sensitive and exquisite performances of Claude Debussy’s Salut Printemps (“Greetings to Spring”) and Einojuhani Rautavaara’s Lapsimessu (“Children’s Mass”). Rautavaara is perhaps the best known and most frequently performed Finnish composer who composed eight symphonies, nine operas, and 12 concertos, as well as numerous vocal and chamber works. “This was our most artistically substantial collaboration with the symphony,” remarked Tuan. “The audience and collaborators were impressed by Ensemble’s skill, sound, and musical sophistication. I enjoyed having the opportunity to conduct the welcoming and incredibly skilled musicians of the Oakland Symphony for the first time,” he said. Under Tuan’s assured direction, singers and orchestra created a breathtaking and engaging performance. Founding Artistic Director Robert Geary expressed the impact: The performances of the Debussy and the Rautavaara rose to the highest artistic standards. Ensemble (flagship group of the Choir) demonstrated again why it has been so successful on national and international stages. Complex musical structures and harmonies were performed effortlessly, intonation was impeccable, and the French and the Latin expertly handled. Maestro Tuan was masterful conducting both the Oakland Symphony and Ensemble. Guest conductor Kalena Bovell led the Symphony through Respighi’s Fountains of Rome with warmth and grace, bringing the listeners on a journey to Rome and the joy and energy of its signature fountains at varying times of day. Bringing the audience to its feet for a third time in the evening’s program, Meng Su delivered a stirring and passionate rendition of Rodrigo’s Concierto de Aranjuez. Throughout the evening, Tuan, Bovell, and representatives of the Oakland Symphony musicians and administration shared loving memories of both Bonnie Bonetti-Bell and the late Oakland Symphony conductor Michael Morgan, who designed the program with Bonnie’s husband, PEBCC Board Treasurer James Bell. “This [was] Bonnie’s playlist. Bonnie’s family name is Bonetti, and she [was] immensely proud of her Italian heritage. Bonnie found her Italian voice in Respighi. She was always thrilled by the Fountains of Rome even when Debussy lives in her heart,” he said. “Both our granddaughters have been enriched by singing in the Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir, and before Bonnie’s transition to her next life, Artistic Director Eric Tuan brought a 13-voice choir to our home to premiere our love song that we commissioned Eric to compose. The singers rehearsed on my driveway and Eric told them, ‘Today is not about perfection; today is about singing from your hearts.’ Eric conducting Lapsimessu [was] a perfect coda to capture Bonnie’s rich spiritual presence,” Bell said. Audiences may join the choirs for a reprise of these works, and premieres by Jens Ibsen and Eric Tuan at their Making History concert this Saturday, March 19 at 7:30 p.m. at the First Congregational Church of Berkeley. Tickets are available at https://www. piedmontchoirs.org/event-calendar.
articles.title: Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir joins Oakland Symphony in Eric Tuan’s triumphant conducting debut

articles.text: San Francisco Playhouse will produce Water by the Spoonful opening March 16 and running to April 23. Winner of the 2012 Pulitzer Prize for Drama, the play written by Quiara Alegría Hudes is a heartfelt meditation on lives on the brink of redemption. Set in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, Eliot has returned from Iraq and is working at a Subway sandwich shop while simultaneously trying to jumpstart his acting career. “Quiara Alegría Hudes’s masterful Pulitzer Prize winner speaks even more profoundly to our world today,” said Bill English, San Francisco Playhouse Artistic Director. “Separated from friends and loved ones by the pandemic, we, like the characters in Water by the Spoonful, celebrate our human resourcefulness, which will overcome any distance to build connection and hope.” The play is directed by Denise Blasor, with performances on the main stage through April 23. Proof of up-to-date vaccination is required to attend. articles.text: Mila Kunis and Justin Timberlake in Friends with Benefits Friends With Benefits is not your grandfather’s movie. In the 1939 film Gone With the Wind Vivien Leigh asks Clark Gable, “What shall I do? Where shall I go?” He turns and says, “Frankly my dear, I don’t give a damn.” That singular word, “damn,” evoked gasps from audiences and represented a sea change in movies. It was the beginning of a gradual loosening of film censorship regarding not only language but the interaction between men and women (physical and verbal). Until the late 1950s, Ozzie and Harriet slept in separate beds and everyone had a robe handy. Decorum and restraint ruled. But that was then, and this is now. Romantic comedies such as Friends definitely represent another change in terms of language and physical contact. True, “FWB” has outstanding portrayals by Mila Kunis as Jamie, young NYC based headhunter, and Justin Timberlake as Dylan, online art director from LA, who arrives in New York for an interview with GQ magazine. And true the exploration of benefits is taken to the edge of that well-worn envelope and beyond. “FWB” is randy and profane and funny, even if it’s a runaway cliché. You know the drill: cool guy and hot girl like each other and swear they can be friends even if they have sex. Neither is looking for a commitment. They have tons of chemistry, hangout well, text, and even find themselves in the middle of a Manhattan flash mob, doing what flash mobs do. It’s all kinda cool. But not to forget: benefits signify benefits. No matter the steam on the windows and their amazing mutual attraction. What Jamie and Dylan refuse to acknowledge – and the story moves from pillar to post in terms of narrative – is what everyone in the audience already knows: they’re in love. Denial (or sustained dissembling when confronted) is not a river in India, but in rom-coms of this ilk it’s a familiar refuge. The tension is nicely developed, compounded by Jamie’s conviction that she’s damaged in some vague way and Dylan’s certainty that he’s emotionally unavailable. Both have been told this during past breakups. As romantic comedies go, and there have been a spate of them in the last several years, “FWB” is the exception, meaning it’s really good. The writing is sharp, the pacing is engaging, and both Jamie and Dylan are smart and interesting, especially Jamie. Kunis is wonderful, and if she is an example of the young, metro woman who is confident and fearless, in a funny, quick, and intelligent way, that’s all to the good. “FWB” is light years from It Happened One Night with Clark Gable and Claudette Colbert (1934), and way better than anything that has appeared recently, including No Strings Attached. Friends With Benefits. Directed by Will Gluck. Starring Mila Kunis, Justin Timberlake, Patricia Clarkson, Richard Jenkins and Jemma Elfman. 1 hr., 49 min. Rated R.

articles.text: Surely it was tempting for the filmmakers to portray an elderly woman who permanently parks her weathered and much lived-in van in a tony neighborhood in North London, as charmingly eccentric. All she needs is an umbrella and wide-brimmed straw hat. While she’s decidedly pungent, dressed in frayed, castoff clothes, she’s also educated. Behind the layer of grime and rags is a fiercely independent, termagant, tart-tongued “bag lady.” Her name is Mary/Margaret Shepherd and as portrayed by Maggie Smith in Lady in the Van, she’s not simply local color, nor does she provide comic relief for the locals. There is more to her than she is willing to tell. She arrives with a history that is only briefly revealed in flashbacks, mere glimpses into her past. But at first glance she seems a harmless vagabond. One of the neighbors, Alan Bennett (Alex Jennings), a playwright and a bit of a recluse himself, grudgingly and against his better judgment, invites Mary to park her van in his driveway – for just a short time while she sorts herself out. As it turns out, Mary stays for 15 years. What Bennett learns as the years slip by is that Mary is not simply a determined gypsy but a deeply damaged human being who is suffering from gradual dementia, abiding health issues, and a sense of overwhelming isolation. She is a mass of contradictions and continues to surprise Bennett as he adjusts to her presence (her van is soon surrounded by plastic bags of garbage and personal detritus). His head-shaking tolerance turns not into anger or regret, but into concern and then affection. He learns that she was once a pianist, a failed nun, and has a brother living just outside of London. She had a life and then lost track of it. And as a writer he can’t help but view Mary as possible material for his work. The Lady in the Van is particularly English, meaning it is a quiet, careful character study of Mary and Alan, and a close depiction of their relationship (a plot is barely discernable). The film is adapted from a memoir published by Bennett in 1989, which became a stage play starring Maggie Smith in 1999, and recently brought to the screen. Smith was the obvious choice for the movie. She brings to the role all of her talent and ability, to include the hauteur of the dowager so central to Downton Abbey, combined with elements of her marvelous portrayal as professor McGonagall in Harry Potter. Maggie Smith is a treasure and is in essence the reason to see this film. It does have an embedded question that has more to do with Bennett than with Smith and that is when confronted with a homeless individual like Mary, what is the right thing to do? His neighbors take an interest in her welfare but always from a distance. Though Alan offers his driveway and gradually his support, he never tries to overcome her choice to live as she does. He takes her as he finds her. His decision keeps the movie from being sentimental or maudlin. And in the end he does tell Mary’s story, such as it is. The Lady in the Van. Directed by Nicholas Hytner. Starring Maggie Smith, Alex Jennings, Roger Allam. 1 hr., 44 min. articles.text: Chris Evans as Captain America in a scene from Captain America: The First Avengers. Who are these pulp fiction superheroes and why do they resonate with our children? Whatever the answer, Hollywood is in love with the comic book genre, especially with tales from the archives of DC and Marvel Comics Summer big tent blockbusters are often defined by the superhero: “Thor”; “X-Men: First Class”; “Green Lantern.” And not to forget “Transformers.” Plus “Harry Potter,” a superhero to be sure. Just ask Voldermort. An example is the 2011 film, Captain America: The First Avenger. Consider the setup: a 90-pound weakling, Steve Rogers (Chris Evans), is desperate to join the Army and fight the Nazis (“I hate bullies” he says), but he can’t pass the physical. He is recruited and transformed (using Super-Soldier serum) into a totally ripped G.I. Joe, aka Captain America, replete with shield, mask and tights. What 90-pound kid wouldn’t love to suddenly have the washboard abs of Captain America, an all-American hero who goes off to fight not just the Nazis, but evil doers in an outfit called Hydra, led by Red Skull (Hugo Weaving), someone who also possess some serious weaponry. This first Captain America was an origin film (begins in 1942), and act one is devoted to how Rogers morphs into his present incarnation. It’s all nicely done, albeit with holes in the logic, requiring serious suspension of disbelief as well as a huge assist by Computer graphics. But then, that’s what defines these wonderfully imagined movies. “No way” some literalists might say. Response: a chorus of kids saying, “Yes, way!” Captain America fights for truth and justice, which means serious combat with the Hydra. Sequel to follow. Captain America: The First Avengers. Director Joe Johnston. Starring Chris Evans, Haley Atwell, Tommy Lee Jones, Hugo Weaving and Stanley Tucci. 2 hrs., 4 min. Rated PG-13.

articles.text: Old Yeller is a classic, family friendly film, released in 1957, and now streaming on Disney+ and Prime. Set in 1869 in post-Civil War frontier Texas, it has at its center a relationship between a boy, Travis Coates (Tommy Kirk), and a stray dog that he names Old Yeller. In the opening scenes we see Travis’ father, Jim (Fess Parker), about to leave for Kansas to buy cattle. While he is gone, Travis and his younger brother, Artiss (Kevin Corcoran), work the cornfields and it’s there that Travis encounters a stray Black Mountain cur. Initially, he tries to chase the dog away, but when it saves his brother from a bear that is defending her cubs, he changes his mind about the courageous dog, and the brothers bring it home, not realizing the impact it will have on their lives. One evening, a neighbor, Bud Searchy (Jeff York), and his granddaughter, Lizbeth, come to dinner and Lisbeth, close to Travis in age, tells him that Old Yeller has been stealing food throughout the county. Hearing this, Travis, concerned, scolds the dog. One day, Old Yeller’s previous owner, Bud Sanderson (Chuck Connors), stops by, looking for the dog. Realizing that the boys have grown attached to the dog, he agrees to swap Old Yeller for a good home cooked meal. Bud also warns the boys that there is a plague of hydrophobia in the area and to keep an eye on their animals, including the dog. Not long thereafter, Old Yeller is attacked by a feral pig and wounded. Concerned, his injury is treated by Travis’ mom, Katie (Dorothy McGuire), and the boy insists that the hog is not rabid. But the threat of rabies remains as a subplot throughout the story. Early one morning, Travis spots their cow, Rose, stumbling about the yard, its mouth foaming, and he is forced to get the family rifle and shoot Rose. Katie and Lizbeth, who is visiting, burn the body; but while disposing of the cow, a wolf comes on the property and attacks them. Old Yeller fights the wolf off, but in the process, is bitten. Katie is certain that the wolf was rabid, and regretfully insists that Old Yeller must be shot. Travis pleads for the dog’s life, suggesting that they put him in a pen and wait to determine if he has any symptoms of the disease. Reluctantly, Katie agrees, and so they wait. The tension builds, and Travis visits the pen daily with hope and food. How the final act turns out is what makes this fine Disney film compelling. Kids, 8 and older and older, will be captivated by the story, made in stunning color with just the right amount of action and heart-rending moments. Old Yeller. Directed by Robert Stevenson. Starring Dorothy McGuire, Tommy Kirk, Fess Parker. 1 hr., 28 min. Rated G. Currently streaming on Prime and Disney. Beverly Washburn, Dorothy McGuiren and Tommy Kirk in Old Yeller.

articles.text: Napa Valley, the nation’s most famous wine growing region, is divided into 16 different agricultural areas called AVA’s. Many of the names like Stag’s Leap, St. Helena and Mount Veeder have become almost as famous as Napa itself. You could also add the Rutherford AVA to that list. The Rutherford AVA is centered around the town of Rutherford in the flat center of Napa Valley and is famous for its high-quality Cabernet Sauvignon. The appellation of 6600 acres consists of gravel, loam, sand and volcanic soils. Rutherford is home to some of Napa’s most historic and iconic wineries such as Inglenook and Beaulieu Vineyards. In February the Rutherford Dust Society, a group of wineries and growers dedicated to promoting the Rutherford AVA, held a tasting at Peju Winery for Trade and Media. Most of the region’s wineries showed up to pour one or more of their wines. Of the many excellent wines poured that day the wines selected below were the cream of the crop – the best of Rutherford AVA. wine’s deep ruby/purple color is followed by sweet, full-bodied flavors, copious quantities of black fruits and a long, lusty finish. A job well done. The Chaix family is in the heart of the Rutherford AVA. • 2018 Chaix Cabernet Sauvignon For many years the Chaix family has been farming grapes in Napa Valley and is now bottling wine under their own name. Their 2018 Cabernet Sauvignon is deep garnet-purple colored and opens with notes of blackberries, plums and cigar box with flavors on the palate of raspberries, currants and black pepper. Medium to full-bodied, it is a rich wine with good structure and a smooth finish. • 2019 Tres Sabores Zinfandel While most of the Rutherford AVA is planted to Cabernet Sauvignon, there is still some Zinfandel left as this bottling shows. Made from 48-year-old vines the wine exhibits superb purity, wonderful fruit, and the classic raspberry/cherry spicy Zinfandel aromatic flavor profile. The Morisoli vineyard is over 100 years old, but this is the first vintage under its name. • 2018 Morisoli Cabernet Sauvignon Rutherford The Morisoli Vineyard was planted in 1902 in the heart of Rutherford. Up until now the grapes were sold to high-quality local producers, but the current generation of the family has decided it’s time to bottle under their own name. This is their first vintage and it’s a winner. It offers up aromas of forest floor, black cherries, earth and spice with the oak pushed to the background. Full-bodied with good depth, richness and density, the tannin is velvety textured and beautifully integrated into this full-throttled Cabernet Sauvignon. Drink over the next 15-20 years. • 2012 Frank Family Lady Edythe Brut Rose Reserve Sparkling Wine Yes, the name of this wine is a mouthful… but so is the wine. Made from 60% Chardonnay and 40% Pinot Noir, this is a late disgorged wine, meaning that is has spent 8 years aging on its lees. This gives amazing complexity to the nose and palate. It has an enchanting combination of citrus along with baked bread aromas. It is clean and fresh in the mouth with layers of flavors. This is one of the finest New World sparkling wines I have tasted. • 2016 Kale McGah Vineyard Red Blend This is 84% Grenache and 16 % Mourvedre which are rare grapes for Rutherford. Medium ruby in color, the McGah opens with crushed strawberries and raspberries with touches of orange peel, underbrush, and spice box. The palate is medium-bodied and intense with a nice spiciness, good frame, and lovely freshness. Crack this open the next time you fire up the BBQ and throw on the ribs.
articles.title: The Best of Rutherford AVA

articles.text: It was another sunny, beautiful day last Wednesday and the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays group responded with 33 members and Siow Fang Tan had shared information about the city’s Heritage Tree program, and the walkers thought it would be fun and informative to go see some of the past Heritage Trees, and also submit a tree candidate of their own. The first past Heritage Tree was an easy one for the walkers to see. They just had to look up at the Highland poplars that surround the Exedra. This is a deciduous tree with a shapely oval form. They are considered to be drought tolerant. Their large, serrated, heart-shaped leaves turn yellow in fall. They are fast growers and will grow to be about 50 feet tall at maturity with a spread of 30 feet. They can live for 60 The next Heritage Tree was a short walk to the Community Hall to see a Yulan Magnolia in the rotunda in front of the building. This tree is native to China and is also called Lilly Magnolia. It was probably the first magnolia cultivated about 4,000 years ago. It has pure white, elegant flowers, and was regarded as far back as 650 AD by Buddhist monks as a symbol of purity. The tree in front of the Community Hall was planted by former Piedmont Public Works superintendent Dave Frankel. Nearby was a set of Japanese maple next to the Japanese Tea House. Unlike many other Piedmont trees, their leaves had not yet emerged. These maples are prized for their delicate and colorful foliage throughout the growing season and autumn. This tree is a smallish and slow growing, with mature heights up to 30 feet. Their leaves offer striking color throughout the growing season, becoming even more beautiful with their fall color change. The next tree was the very tall California redwood just inside the old columns of Frank C. Havens’ Wildwood Estate in Wildwood Gardens. This is a massive tree that has been watered by an underwater creek for decades. This is an evergreen species that can live 1,200 to 2,200 years or more. They are among the oldest living things on earth and also the tallest trees, reaching up to 379 feet in height without the roots and up to 29 feet in diameter. The species is monoecious, with pollen and seed cones on the same plant. The walkers loved this tree and stopped for a group photo in front of it. The walkers then went to the Hall Fenway at the corner of Wildwood and Crocker Avenue to see a set of European white birch trees. This is a short-lived species native to northern North America. pages.text: 22 Wednesday, March 16, 2022 Walking on Wednesday Wednesday Walkers tour the city’s Heritage Trees By Dick Carter It was another sunny, beautiful day last Wednesday and the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays group responded with 33 members and one K-9 best friend. Siow Fang Tan had shared information about the city’s Heritage Tree program, and the walkers thought it would be fun and informative to go see some of the past Heritage Trees, and also submit a tree candidate of their own. The first past Heritage Tree was an easy one for the walkers to see. They just had to look up at the Highland poplars that surround the Exedra. This is a deciduous tree with a shapely oval form. They are considered to be drought tolerant. Their large, serrated, heart-shaped leaves turn yellow in fall. They are fast growers and will grow to be about 50 feet tall at maturity with a spread of 30 feet. They can live for 60 years or more. The next Heritage Tree was a short walk to the Community Hall to see a Yulan Magnolia in the rotunda in front of the building. This tree is native to China and is also called Lilly Magnolia. It was probably the first magnolia cultivated about 4,000 years ago. It has pure white, elegant flowers, and was regarded as far back as 650 AD by Buddhist monks as a symbol of purity. The tree in front of the Community Hall was planted by former Piedmont Public Works superintendent Dave Frankel. Nearby was a set of Japanese maple next to the Japanese Tea House. Unlike many other Piedmont trees, their leaves had not yet emerged. These maples are prized for their delicate and colorful foliage throughout the growing season and autumn. This tree is a smallish and slow growing, with mature heights up to 30 feet. Their leaves offer striking color throughout the growing season, becoming even more beautiful with their fall color change. The next tree was the very tall California redwood just inside the old columns of Frank C. Havens’ Wildwood Estate in Wildwood Gardens. This is a massive tree that has been watered by an underwater creek for decades. This is an evergreen species that can live 1,200 to 2,200 years or more. They are among the oldest living things on earth and also the tallest trees, reaching up to 379 feet in height without the roots and up to 29 feet in diameter. The species is monoecious, with pollen and seed cones on the same plant. The walkers loved this tree and stopped for a group photo in front of it. The walkers then went to the Hall Fenway at the corner of Wildwood and Crocker Avenue to see a set of European white birch trees. This is a short-lived species native to northern North America. Its thin, white bark peels in paper like layers from the trunk. The wood is often used for pulpwood and firewood. It is a medium-sized deciduous tree typically reaching 66 feet tall, and exceptionally to 130 feet with a trunk up to 30 inches in diameter. This tree is a typically short-lived species, but in colder-climate regions can grow for more than 100 years. Its fall color is a bright yellow. The next tree was a Monterey pine across the street in Crocker Park. This tree is native to the Central Coast of California and Mexico. It is an evergreen and is a versatile, fast-growing, medium-density softwood, suitable for a wide range of uses. It is the most widely cultivated pine in the world, and is also the most widely planted tree for choose-and-cut Christmas tree farms in California. Its root system can extend 30 to 39 feet. They grow to between 50 and 100 feet in height in the wild, and up to 200 feet in cultivation. They attain full size in 80 to 100 years, but rarely live beyond 150 years. Some walkers remembered one of these Crocker Park pines coming down a few years ago in a windstorm and falling onto Hampton Road. The next tree was a grove of huge eucalyptus trees on Hampton where St. James Drive ends. Eucalyptus trees are also known as gum trees, and are native to Australia, which has almost 900 species of them. They are found throughout California and have become invasive along the coast. They grow rapidly, and many species attain great height. The giant gum tree is one of the largest and can grow to about 300 feet and have a circumference of about 25 feet. A eucalyptus tree can grow six feet each year. They can have long lives with most species able to survive 250 years. Their wood is sometimes used as a less expensive and more easily and sustainably farmed hardwood. Eucalyptus leaves are also poisonous to most animals and humans. Eucalyptus trees got here as seeds on ships coming to California from Australia in the 1850s during the Gold Rush. Within a few decades of them being planted on the West Coast, many Californians grew disenchanted with them. The trees proved to be terrible for woodworking, and the wood often split and cracked, making it a poor choice for railroad ties. The trees were also thirsty and drained wells. They are filled with aromatic oil, which makes them highly combustible. In the East Bay firestorm of 1991, vast swaths of eucalyptus burned, and the fire left 25 people dead and thousands homeless. The walkers had now seen all their Heritage Tree candidates and it was time to vote. The California redwood won in a landslide. It received all but one vote. With the voting done it was time for return to the town center. Noemi Alvarado and Siow Fang Tan volunteered to make a Walking on Wednesdays’ submission for a Heritage Tree. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the Group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation is required at https:// tinyurl.com/3ethkehu. articles.text: Members of the First Mondays Reading Group on the deck at the Japanese Tea House in Piedmont Park: Bella Almanzan (left), Ken Young, Adrienne Hamlin, Carol Long, Lois Price, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Sarah Johnson, Karin Fetherston, Darby Gragg, Mike Bandrowski, Jerry Gragg, Melba Yee, Pat McMahon, Laura Goldman, Mike Henn, Albert Chen, and Priscilla Wanerus. Piedmont Recreation Department’s First Mondays Reading Group met again outside the Tea House in the Piedmont Park on March 7. It was another warm, sunny afternoon and 18 members of the group were on hand for the discussion without the need for masks. Carol Long continued to spoil the group with candy and fruit, which were of light blue and yellow colors to honor the Ukrainian people. The group was there to discuss their March selection, Matt Haig’s The Midnight Library. a fantasy best-selling novel published in 2020. Haig’s protagonist is Nora Seed, a young woman who is unhappy with her life choices and is filled with regrets. Everything possible in her life is bad, including a lost job and a dead cat. During the night she tries to kill herself but ends up in a library managed by her old school librarian. The library is between life and death with millions of books filled with stories of different versions of Nora’s life. She can visit as many as she wants to find out what her life would have been if she had made different decisions. She gets to find her perfect life and finally be happy. But none satisfies her. The things that are making her unhappy in her “root life” go with her to other lives. However, in this process she eventually finds that her existence really does matter. She has significant, often unintended, positive effects on others. Additionally, she has the potential to build a brighter future with her actual life. She doesn’t need a new life, she just needs to realize that her own life has potential, and she could keep reinventing herself until she achieves happiness. The Midnight Library turned out to be a surprisingly good book group selection because some readers loved it, and others didn’t like it at all. This made for a good conversation. Those on the positive side appreciated the moral that life does matter. You have the ability to affect others, and you have the potential to keep working towards happiness for yourself and others. It was noted that at the age of 24 Haig experienced severe depression and an attempted suicide, so his writing seems to be an attempt to help others work through difficult times. Those who did not care for the book found the character of Nora to be shallow and gave up too easily on her loves and lives. Learning of Haig’s personal history led to a discussion of how much a reader should know about the author before reading the Matt Haig’s The Midnight Library work. It was agreed that a book needs to stand on its own. With their discussion complete the group turned to future book selections. They had previously picked the non-fiction Destiny of the Republic by Candice Millard as their April book and The Lincoln Highway by Amor Towles for May. The next discussion will be Monday, April 4 at 1:30 p.m. with plans to meet outside the Japanese Tea House in the park. New readers are welcome to join the group and there is no fee to participate. Registration is required by calling 510 420-3070 to register.

pages.text: 26 Wednesday, March 16, 2022 Girl Webelos advance to Scouting Webelos is the most-advanced level of Cub Scouting. On February 8, the six 5th-grade girl Webelos based at Havens School transitioned to Scouting in a ceremony called Arrow of Light. New Scouts Charli Hale, Dani Hale, Lauren “Mai” Levy, Ashlan Mitchell, Willow Thomas and Molly Tulloch crossed over to the Bobcat Patrol in Piedmont Council’s Troop 15 during a Court of Honor. Other Webelos to join Troop 15 in the past year include Kai Hsu, John Bunje, Quinton Cole, and Rafael “Rafa” Rajan. After just one month in Scouting, Molly Tulloch said, “Troop 15 is really fun. I’m looking forward to camping trips and working on merit badges.” Patrol Leader Christiane Zuber was recognized at the Court of Honor for her leadership to the Bobcats. She, too, was once a Webelo in Pack 3 at Havens. “Bobcats like camping and learning new skills”, she explained. “For Summer Camp, we are going to Emerald Bay on Catalina Island from June 18-25. I’m going to learn to canoe and kayak on the sea.” Girls and boys ages 11 and up and their parents with an interest in spending time in nature and improving leadership skills can learn more about Scouting by attending the Troop 15 Open House on Tuesday, March 22 at 7:30 pm at Havens School, 325 Highland Avenue. For more information, contact Scoutmaster Glen Tripp at Glen@Galileo-learning.com. articles.text: On Sunday afternoon, March 6, a man brandishing, what turned out to be a replica gun, in the Trestle Glen area led the Piedmont police to issue a shelter-in-place notice to nearby residents and the deployment of an Oakland police helicopter. The first call to police occurred at 3:20 p.m. about a man wearing a black hooded sweatshirt, red Chicago Bulls jersey, and dark pants waving a gun while walking on Trestle Glen Road. The man was initially scared off by a barking dog before walking up the steps to Sandringham Road. Three more calls to police came in from St James Drive, Cambrian Way and Sandringham Road about a man mumbling to himself and entering a resident’s backyard. Piedmont police issued a shelter in place order to residents in the area. Alameda County Sheriff’s Office and Oakland Police provided additional support and an Oakland Police Department helicopter was seen in the area, trying to locate the man. The suspect unlawfully entered a garage on St. James Drive and was confronted by the homeowner as he was rummaging through cabinets. The suspect, identified as Miguel Mejia, 31, of Oakland, was taken into custody by police and the gun was determined to be a replica. Piedmont Police’s investigation found that Mejia pointed the replica weapon on three different occasions at three separate residents. The shelter-in-place lasted approximately 90 minutes. Mejia was arrested and transported to Santa Rita jail. He was on a felony probation with a full search clause and was charged with home invasion, burglary, brandishing a weapon, trespassing and probation violations. March 15. articles.text: A Mother-Daughter event hosted by Girl Scout Troop 31765 returns this year on April 24 at 1 p.m. at the Veterans Hall, 401 Highland Avenue. Girls and their mothers and grandmothers are invited to enjoy a delightful tea service and paint a tea cup and saucer while sharing the companionship of the favorite women in their lives. Guests will receive a complimentary photograph, patch and favor. All ages are welcome; guests do not need to be a registered Girl Scout. COVID protocols are in place and space is limited. The fee is $60 for the first couple and $25 for each additional guest. Email yeh4mom@ yahoo.com for registration or questions. Painting teacups and saucers. Girl Scout Troop 31765 hosts the Mother-Daughter event in 2019.

articles.text: This year’s trip has been scaled back due to COVID precautions, despite immense popularity and desire for participation. This spring the church is anticipating 160 students and 40 adult volunteers traveling to Tijuana to build 12 homes for families in need. Two years ago, 270 students and 25 adults signed up to build 18 homes before the trip was canceled. Mexico trip volunteers will set up tents and camp between Tijuana and Tecate, four miles south of the U.S. border. The houses are built for the least fortunate residents in Tijuana, many living in shelters made of cardboard. The students forego a typical spring break vacation to serve others, and often return transformed by the experience. Piedmont residents donated over 2,000 items to the church for the Treasures Sale. The popular Treasures Sale at PCC raised over $19,000 for the Youth Service Trip to build houses in Mexico.
